1.grade_fit_note: Proximity agreement with neither/nor plus a tense-shift site (L.5.1d) is right for grade 5; the proximity rule is the harder half.
1.note: Verb agrees with the nearer subject (sisters -> were); 'started' fixes past tense, so 'drove'. Clean 2x2.

2.grade_fit_note: Plural possessive and its/it's are grade 3-4 conventions (L.3.2d, L.4.1g); not a grade 7 discriminator.
2.note: 'three teams' coaches' and possessive 'its'. Sound item but targeted three grades too high.

3.grade_fit_note: Kinship words as names vs after a possessive is typically taught by grade 4-5.
3.note: 'Grandpa' is used as a name (no possessive); 'my uncle' is not. Key is the mixed cell (see _batch).

4.grade_fit_note: Quoted fragment vs quoted full sentence capitalization is a reasonable late-middle-school item; could sit at 6-7.
4.note: Integrated fragment 'with real heart' stays lowercase; the full quoted sentence after 'added,' is capitalized.

6.grade_fit_note: Historical period proper noun vs ordinal century is a good grade 6-7 contrast.
6.note: Middle Ages is a named era; 'sixteenth century' is lowercase in Chicago and AP.

7.grade_fit_note: Comma before a tag question is L.5.2c.
7.free_elimination: B and D end a sentence that ends in 'don't they' with a period; any student who knows questions take a question mark (grade 1 knowledge) kills them without the tag-comma rule.
7.note: Effectively a two-option item (A vs C) because the end-mark axis is near-free at grade 5.

8.grade_fit_note: Coordinate adjectives with no comma before the noun (L.7.2a) is on grade; the irregular plural possessive half is easier (grade 3-4).
8.note: No comma between last adjective and noun; 'children's'. The possessive axis is easy, so the item rests on the comma axis.

9.grade_fit_note: Relative adverbs when/where are L.4.1a; 'which she painted pictures' sounds wrong to most readers.
9.note: 'the week when', 'the cabin where'. Placed three grades high for the standard it tests; B (which/which) is implausible.

10.grade_fit_note: Coordinate vs cumulative adjectives is L.7.2a exactly.
10.note: 'long, exhausting' coordinate; 'two tall pine' cumulative. D (no comma at all) is a weak defense only under a loose 'short adjectives may skip the comma' practice; not mainstream for a test key.

11.grade_fit_note: Languages vs general school subjects is a standard grade 5-6 rule.
11.note: English is a language (capitalized); geography is not.

12.grade_fit_note: Dangling modifier is L.7.1c; although...but redundancy is a common middle-school error.
12.note: Opener must modify Talia, not her hands; 'although' takes no 'but'. Clean 2x2.

13.grade_fit_note: Parentheses and nonrestrictive commas are L.6.2a.
13.free_elimination: C and D have an unpaired comma (closing comma after 'contest' with no opening comma after 'class'); a student who knows commas around an inserted clause come in pairs kills both without deciding restrictive vs nonrestrictive.
13.note: No comma after the parenthetical (it would split subject and verb); 'which had won' is nonrestrictive and needs both commas.

14.grade_fit_note: Restrictive vs nonrestrictive clauses are on grade 6-7 (L.6.2a).
14.free_elimination: B and C open a comma before 'who runs the school garden' and never close it; pairing alone kills them.
14.note: 'Only the students who finished' is restrictive (no commas); 'who runs the school garden' is nonrestrictive and must be closed before 'plant'.

15.grade_fit_note: Proper adjectives with a common noun is grade 5-7 material; fine at 7 though slightly easy.
15.note: Proper adjectives Japanese/Canadian capitalized; 'garden' is common. 'Japanese Garden' would only be right as a named place, which the sentence does not set up.

16.grade_fit_note: Pronoun case and intensive pronouns are L.6.1a-b exactly.

17.grade_fit_note: Pronoun shift (L.6.1d) and case with an appositive noun.

18.grade_fit_note: Region vs compass direction is a grade 5-6 rule.
18.note: 'the American Southwest' is a region; 'drove east' is a direction.

19.grade_fit_note: Perfect tense and inappropriate tense shift are L.5.1b-d.
19.note: 'had eaten' (participle) and 'was reading' (past). 'had ate' is a real dialect error, so A/D are plausible.

20.grade_fit_note: Street names and common nouns are grade 2-4 capitalization.
20.note: 'Cedar Avenue' is a name; 'small lake' is common. 'small Lake' is unlikely to attract a fifth grader.

21.grade_fit_note: Semicolon between independent clauses plus comma after an introductory subordinate clause; on grade or slightly above (semicolons formally L.9-10.2a).
21.note: Comma after the 'Although' clause; semicolon joins the two independent clauses (B is a comma splice).

22.grade_fit_note: Subjunctive and mood shifts are L.8.1c-d exactly.
22.note: 'I wish I were' and 'if I had practiced'. D's 'I wish I was' is recognised in descriptive usage guides (e.g. Merriam-Webster usage notes) as common informal standard; formal test grammar keys A.

23.grade_fit_note: Commas in a series (L.5.2a) with a subject-verb comma trap.
23.note: Series commas after 'zipper' and 'bags'; no comma between the compound subject and 'were'. All options use the serial comma, so AP vs Chicago does not split it.

24.note: Short article 'the' lowercase inside a title; verb 'Was' capitalized (Chicago, AP, APA, MLA all agree). The title is not italicized, which is a rendering limitation, not a defect in the tested choice.

_batch: Keys are flat (A, B, C, D six each) and there are no length or wording tells, but there is a strong cross-item structural tell on the count axis. In all 8 Capitalization items (3, 4, 6, 11, 15, 18, 20, 24) the key is the mixed cell: exactly one of the two sites is capitalized and the other is lowercase; the all-capitals and all-lowercase options are never the key. The same holds for most punctuation items where the axis is mark-present vs mark-absent: 10, 13, 14, 21 and 23 key the option with a mark at one site and none (or the other mark) at the other, and 8 keys the option with the middle comma count. Only item 7 (both marks present) and item 2 (apostrophe placement, not presence) break it. A test-wise student who notices that 'extreme' options (most marks/capitals, fewest marks/capitals) never win can eliminate two options on roughly 14 of the 16 mechanics items without knowing a rule, leaving a 50% guess. This looks like a side-effect of a rule forbidding count-extreme keys: applied uniformly, it makes the extremes reliably dead. Fix by letting some keys be the all-capitalized or no-extra-mark cell (e.g., two proper nouns both capitalized; two restrictive clauses with no commas). Separately, items 13 and 14 allow free elimination through unpaired commas, and item 7 through the end-mark axis. The Grammar/Parts of Speech items (1, 5, 9, 12, 16, 17, 19, 22) show no cross-item pattern.
